title: Telangana Orders Statewide IVF Probe After 43 Women Rescued From Egg Racket
excerpt: Inspections of 27 of Telangana's 44 fertility facilities have found 13 violations at seven hospitals, as the women's commission questions five named centres over the alleged illegal egg-collection network busted in Hyderabad on October 31.
body:
• Telangana Health Minister C. Damodar Rajanarasimha has ordered a comprehensive investigation into the alleged illegal collection of human eggs, after a Hyderabad racket was busted on October 31 with eight arrests and 43 women rescued.
  • Task-force inspections have covered 27 of the state's 44 assisted reproductive technology facilities; officials found 13 regulatory violations at seven hospitals and issued show-cause notices.
  • The Telangana State Commission for Women has separately questioned five named fertility centres — Indira IVF, Narmada Fertility, Oasis Fertility, Sadguru ART and Padmaja Fertility — and ordered written explanations.
  • Anyone approached by an intermediary offering money for egg donation can report it to their district medical and health officer; under the ART Act, 2021, egg donation requires written consent and prescribed medical safeguards.

Telangana's health minister has ordered a comprehensive investigation into the alleged illegal collection of human oocytes, widening a crackdown that began with a Hyderabad police bust on October 31 in which eight people were arrested and 43 women were rescued, according to an India Today report of a Press Trust of India account of an official release. The minister, C. Damodar Rajanarasimha, directed officials to take stringent action against institutions and individuals found violating regulations.

Inspections Find Violations at Seven Hospitals

Following the minister's directions, task-force groups intensified inspections of IVF centres across Telangana. Officials have so far inspected 27 of the 44 assisted reproductive technology (ART) facilities identified in the state, and found 13 regulatory violations at seven hospitals, whose managements have been issued show-cause notices. Inspections of the remaining facilities are under way.

Further action is expected after officials examine records seized by police and information sought from the National Assisted Reproductive Technology and Surrogacy Registry. State health officials visited the registry in New Delhi on November 6 to seek data submitted by registered ART clinics and banks in Telangana. The investigation is examining the roles of the women identified in the case, doctors, IVF centres and intermediaries, the release said.

Five Fertility Centres Questioned by Women's Commission

In a parallel track, the Telangana State Commission for Women issued notices to five fertility centres over allegations of illegal egg collection, and the managing directors, medical superintendents and heads of the centres appeared before the commission at its Buddha Bhavan office on Monday, Hyderabad Mail reported. The centres named were Indira IVF Centre, Narmada Fertility Centre, Oasis Fertility Centre, Sadguru ART Centre and Padmaja Fertility Centre. The commission directed them to submit written explanations to chairperson Sharada Nerella.

The inquiry will examine whether the centres violated the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021, which mandates written consent from egg donors, medical safeguards and compliance with prescribed limits on egg retrieval. Days earlier, the commission had publicly expressed dissatisfaction with the pace of action, noting that women who came forward had named the five centres and a physician identified as Dr. Hussain, against whom no case had then been registered.

How the Racket Allegedly Worked

Police allege the accused recruited women from West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh and other states, transported them to Hyderabad and housed them in rented premises in areas including Prakash Nagar, Begumpet, Erragadda, Saroornagar and Gopalapuram, according to Hyderabad Mail's account of the Malkajgiri police investigation. The women told investigators they had been administered hormone injections and medication, and police intervened before the operation proceeded to egg retrieval and supply to fertility centres. Nine people were apprehended in the raids and the accused are in judicial remand, the report said.

The state health minister has separately directed that registrations of IVF centres found involved in illegal procurement be permanently cancelled and that officials examine revoking the medical licences of complicit doctors. An expert committee is to be formed to recommend stronger enforcement of the ART and Surrogacy Acts in the state.

What the Health Department Is Telling Women

The health department said oocyte collection must be carried out in accordance with the ART Act and its rules, and that every ART clinic and bank operating in the state must hold the required registration. It advised women not to accept misleading assurances or financial inducements from intermediaries, which could expose them to unauthorised medical procedures, and urged the public to report suspected illegal activity to the district medical and health officer concerned.

For diaspora readers who travel to India for fertility treatment, the case underlines a practical check: a clinic's ART registration and written-consent process are the first things to verify before any procedure. The investigation is continuing, and the commission has said it will scrutinise the centres' explanations and the available evidence before deciding on further action.
